questions.question: In a zkVM, what is an execution trace?
options: A table of witness values per step of execution
A Merkle tree root of the program source code
A single polynomial that directly encodes the whole program
A set of elliptic-curve points used for a trusted setup
questions.explanation: zkVMs typically record execution as a step-indexed table (registers, memory buses, etc.) and then prove the table satisfies constraints.

questions.question: What does the sumcheck protocol help a verifier do efficiently?
options: Verify a claimed sum of a multivariate polynomial over the Boolean hypercube
Compute a SHA-256 hash faster using field arithmetic
Encrypt the witness so the verifier can never learn any values
Derive a trusted setup for KZG commitments
questions.explanation: Sumcheck reduces a large hypercube sum claim to a small number of rounds plus one final evaluation check.

questions.question: In `mle_eval`, why do we fold pairs `(a0, a1)` into `(1-r)*a0 + r*a1`?
options: It fixes one Boolean variable of the multilinear polynomial to the field value r
It converts a multivariate polynomial into a univariate polynomial by FFT
It hides the witness values by blinding with r
It computes a Merkle root over the evaluation table
questions.explanation: For a multilinear polynomial, restricting one variable to r linearly interpolates between its values at 0 and 1, shrinking the table by half each fold.

questions.question: What is the per-round verifier check for multilinear (degree-1) sumcheck messages when the prover sends `(s0, s1)`?
options: Check that `s0 + s1 == current_claim` (mod p)
Check that `s0 * s1 == current_claim` (mod p)
Check that `s0 == s1` to ensure degree-1
Check that `s0` equals the final polynomial evaluation at r
questions.explanation: Each round’s univariate is the partial sum polynomial; at X in {0,1}, the sum must match the running claim, so `s0+s1` must equal the claim.

questions.question: Why does the lesson multiply the per-step violation by `gamma^t` before summing?
options: To make cancellation across different step indices unlikely for a wrong trace
To guarantee perfect zero-knowledge for the trace without commitments
To reduce the proof size from O(log n) to O(1)
To ensure all violations are nonnegative integers
questions.explanation: A geometric weighting turns the sum into a polynomial in gamma; if the violation vector is nonzero, it only hits 0 for a small fraction of gamma values.

questions.question: What is a key difference between what sumcheck proves and what a polynomial commitment (PCS) opening proves?
options: Sumcheck proves a sum claim; PCS openings prove an evaluation claim at a point
Sumcheck is only for hashes; PCS openings are only for encryption
Sumcheck requires a trusted setup; PCS openings never do
Sumcheck only works over real numbers; PCS openings only over integers
questions.explanation: Sumcheck reduces global statements to a final evaluation; a PCS is what makes that final evaluation check verifiable without revealing the full polynomial.

questions.question: Which bug is most likely if the evaluation-table order (LSB/MSB) does not match the folding order in `mle_eval`?
options: The verifier ends up checking a different polynomial than the prover intended
The field modulus becomes composite during execution
The proof becomes interactive again even with Fiat–Shamir
The trace becomes constant-time automatically
questions.explanation: Index-to-bit ordering defines which entries are paired in each fold; a mismatch changes the polynomial being evaluated and can break correctness or soundness.

questions.question: In a Fiat–Shamir transcript, why is it important to include (bind to) a commitment to the trace/polynomials before deriving challenges?
options: So the prover cannot choose challenges after seeing them and adapt the witness
So the verifier can skip all checks except the final one
So the hash function output becomes uniformly distributed over integers
So the protocol works even if the field has size 2
questions.explanation: Binding challenges to the committed witness prevents a prover from tailoring the witness to the challenges, which would break soundness.
